## Export conventions and scope

- These are exports of five located project sessions, not reconstructed or invented conversations. The earliest recorded project exchange is August 13, 2026 in Asia/Manila. The latest included project-build session ends on October 2, 2026. The later conversation used to assemble this export is outside that research-session scope.
- System and developer instructions, private internal reasoning, approval-review agents, token counters and other runtime bookkeeping are excluded. Environment blocks inserted by the client are excluded. User clarification replies and attachment references are retained.
- Context compaction occurs in the Codex source logs. Earlier recorded prompts and visible responses are still exported from the session files. Internal summaries are not presented as verbatim conversation. This package cannot recover turns or attachments that were never saved locally, deleted, or omitted by the original clients.
- Full recorded tool outputs are retained in the JSONL files. Any truncation already present in a source tool result remains present and is not filled in. Local paths in messages are retained as historical references; externally referenced files and links are not automatically downloaded or copied. Binary content already inside recorded tool results stays in those records.
- The user's no-em-dash instruction is applied to text throughout this export: that punctuation is replaced with ` - `. Other message wording is preserved except identified credential redactions. Therefore the readable files are a documented text-normalized export, not a byte-identical copy of the source logs.
- Recognizable credential strings are replaced with `[REDACTED CREDENTIAL]` if found. Redaction and punctuation-replacement counts are recorded in the manifest. Source files were read without modifying them.
- No claim is made that these five sessions cover every AI interaction by every group member. Conversations from other accounts or devices would need to be added from their original exports. No missing exchanges have been invented.

## Human review and course policy

The course requirements call for disclosure of AI tools and complete prompts and responses. They also prohibit directly submitting AI-written code and require students to validate responses and explain their decisions and implementation.

These records include AI-generated code and editing assistance. Creating this transcript does not establish that the students independently rewrote that code, verified every citation, or completed the required human review. The group must check those requirements against its actual work before submission. The saved logs and final project artifacts provide the evidence for reported training and test results.

## Proposal 1: Microscopic Hyperspectral Choledoch Dataset

### Proposal-ready title

**Leakage-Aware Spectral Band Reduction for Efficient Cholangiocarcinoma Segmentation in Microscopic Hyperspectral Images**

### Dataset

The original dataset contains 880 scenes from 174 individuals:

- 689 scenes containing partial cancer areas.
- 49 fully cancerous scenes.
- 142 non-cancer scenes.
- 60 spectral bands from 550–1000 nm.
- HSI resolution of approximately 1280×1024 per band.
- Paired RGB images and polygon annotations created by pathologists.

These details are documented in the original [IEEE Access dataset paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8869757) and subsequent [SAHIS-Net study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11161366/).

Current accessibility is mixed:

- The [original ECNU site](https://bio-hsi.ecnu.edu.cn/) currently responds with a registration/login form, so it is not completely dead, but authorization still needs to be tested.
- The [Kaggle raw mirror](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ethelzq/multidimensional-choledoch-database) is about 103 GB and states that it contains only part of the original data.
- A [preprocessed Kaggle version](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/hfutybx/mhsi-choledoch-dataset-preprocessed-dataset) is about 10.6 GB.
- Recent experiments commonly use a 538-image, 256×320 preprocessed subset, which makes the project substantially more manageable. A 2025 study documents that exact setup and dataset link [here](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/20/3979).

### Research question

> Can a small, carefully selected set of spectral bands retain most of the tumor-segmentation performance of the full 60-band hyperspectral image while reducing memory use and inference time?

A second, particularly valuable question is:

> How much does random scene-level splitting overestimate performance compared with specimen-level splitting?

The filenames reportedly include a tissue-specimen identifier. You should split by that identifier before generating patches. First verify with the dataset administrator whether one specimen identifier maps cleanly to one individual.

### Recommended experiment

Use one identical, understandable 2-D U-Net across all conditions:

- Single-band baseline.
- Three-band false-colour baseline.
- PCA to three components, fitted using training data only.
- Three selected bands.
- Six selected bands.
- Twelve selected bands.
- All 60 bands.

For selection, use a manageable training-only method such as mutual information plus redundancy filtering. You do not need to invent an enormous network.

Primary split:

- Grouped training set by specimen.
- Grouped validation set.
- Completely held-out grouped test set.
- Three random training seeds.
- If time permits, grouped cross-validation.

Never generate patches first and then split the patches. That would let nearly identical regions from the same specimen enter both training and testing.

Report:

- Dice coefficient.
- Mean IoU.
- Precision and recall.
- Boundary F1 or HD95.
- Per-image results and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
- Parameter count.
- Peak GPU memory.
- Inference latency.
- Model size.

### Why it could become a strong paper

Recent medical-HSI research is actively investigating:

- Label-efficient and semi-supervised segmentation, including a [MICCAI 2025 method tested on Choledoch](https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2025/0033-Paper1142.html).
- Spectral–spatial factorization and compact models.
- Spectral band reduction.
- Foundation-model integration, such as the [MICCAI 2025 SAMSA hyperspectral segmentation framework](https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2025/0804-Paper1453.html).
- Evaluation under limited medical data.

Your work would fit these trends without trying to reproduce a PhD-scale architecture.

### Important risks

1. **Annotation quality:** A recent study found that some original masks were too coarse for precise semantic segmentation and reannotated only 94 images. This means boundary errors may partly reflect annotation noise, not model failure. Do not clinically “correct” masks yourself without a pathologist. Document the limitation instead. [Source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11220190/)

2. **Dataset subsets differ:** Papers report 538, 689, 872, or 880 images depending on preprocessing and task. State exactly which files you received and publish a manifest or hashes.

3. **Raw HSI is not a normal JPEG:** The web app should accept a `.npy`, `.mat`, or paired `.raw`/`.hdr` input, render a false-colour preview, then overlay the mask. Confirm this satisfies the professor’s “image upload” requirement.

4. **Compute:** A lightweight 2-D network at 256×320 should be manageable on a 12–16 GB GPU. Full-resolution 3-D training is not a sensible solo scope.

5. **Clinical claims:** Call it a segmentation benchmark or computer-aided analysis method - not a diagnostic system ready for hospitals.

### Verdict

**Doable: 7/10.**  
**Difficulty: ambitious but reasonable.**  
**Publication ceiling: the highest of the three, provided the splitting and statistics are rigorous.**

## Proposal 2: PolypGen

### Proposal-ready title

**Cross-Centre Robust and Lightweight Polyp Segmentation Using Realistic Endoscopic Artifact Augmentation**

### Why this is the best balance

PolypGen contains masks and bounding boxes from six medical centres in Europe and Africa. It was specifically created to study generalization across hospitals, devices, populations, and acquisition conditions.

It includes:

- 1,537 curated single-frame polyp images.
- 2,225 positive sequence frames.
- 4,275 negative frames.
- Pixel masks and Pascal VOC bounding boxes.
- Centre and sequence organization.
- A CC BY 4.0 research dataset available after creating a Synapse account.

The original technical validation trained on 1,449 frames from centres C1–C5 and tested on 88 single frames plus 432 sequence frames from unseen centre C6. That is almost perfect for your professor’s unseen-test requirement. [Scientific Data descriptor](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-01981-y)

### Research question

> Does realistic endoscopy-artifact augmentation improve segmentation on a completely unseen medical centre without making the model too slow for interactive deployment?

Augmentations could simulate:

- Motion blur.
- Defocus.
- Specular highlights.
- Gamma and illumination shifts.
- Compression artifacts.
- Bubbles or partial occlusion.

### Experiment

- U-Net as the transparent baseline.
- One lightweight modern model, such as SegFormer-B0 or DeepLabV3+ with a small backbone.
- Standard augmentation versus artifact-aware augmentation.
- Train on C1–C4.
- Use C5 for validation.
- Lock all decisions.
- Test once on C6.
- Keep sequence/video frames together to prevent leakage.

Report Dice, IoU, HD95, recall, false-positive rate on negative frames, inference latency, and model size.

Current polyp research increasingly emphasizes domain generalization because same-hospital scores often fail on new hospitals and endoscopes. This limitation was demonstrated clearly in the [EndoCV multi-centre evaluation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-52063-x).

### Verdict

**Doable: 9/10.**  
**Scientific quality: excellent.**  
**Main downside:** polyp segmentation is crowded, so the unseen-centre evaluation must be the centre of the contribution.

If Choledoch access fails, this is the dataset I would choose.

## Proposal 3: TrashCan-Material

### Proposal-ready title

**Long-Tail and Degradation-Robust Real-Time Instance Segmentation of Underwater Marine Debris**

### Dataset

TrashCan contains 7,212 underwater images with instance masks and bounding boxes. It includes trash, remotely operated vehicles, and marine flora/fauna. It has:

- A 16-class material taxonomy.
- A 22-class object-instance taxonomy.
- COCO-style instance segmentation annotations.
- A manageable download size compared with hyperspectral imaging.

The official [University of Minnesota TrashCan page](https://irvlab.cs.umn.edu/resources/trashcan) explains the collection and annotations.

### Research question

> Can class-balanced training and realistic underwater degradation augmentation improve rare-class mask accuracy while retaining real-time inference?

### Experiment

Use the 16-class material version because it is less fragmented.

- Small one-stage instance-segmentation model.
- Standard training baseline.
- Class-balanced sampling or focal loss.
- Underwater colour, haze, blur, backscatter, and low-light augmentations.
- Original dataset validation set held out as final test.
- Split the original training portion into training and validation.
- If video/source identifiers are available, group by source video rather than random image.

Report:

- Box mAP@.5:.95.
- Mask mAP@.5:.95.
- Per-class recall.
- Rare-class performance.
- FPS and latency.
- Model size.
- Performance under synthetic corruptions.

The web demo would be very strong: upload a normal underwater image and show masks, labels, counts, and confidence. The current IEEE IPAS 2027 call even includes a special session on AI-driven waste management. [IEEE event page](https://events.vtools.ieee.org/m/563249)

### Verdict

**Doable: 9.5/10.**  
**Best live demo and safest completion.**  
**Main downside:** it needs strong long-tail or robustness analysis to rise above a normal “trained YOLO on a dataset” class project.

## Realistic IEEE route

For a medical topic, [IEEE ISBI 2027](https://biomedicalimaging.org/2027/) is unusually well aligned:

- Four-page full-paper deadline: **October 26, 2026**.
- Conference: May 25–28, 2027, Lausanne.
- Full papers undergo peer review and are considered for publication and presentation.
- The author instructions require ethical-compliance and conflict-of-interest statements. [Submission instructions](https://biomedicalimaging.org/2027/papers/)

That deadline is only 24 days after your class deadline, so it is possible but aggressive. You would need your professor or another faculty member actively reviewing the work before October.

For TrashCan, [IEEE IPAS 2027](https://events.vtools.ieee.org/m/563249) lists a November 10, 2026 submission deadline and a waste-management special session. Verify the final 2027 publication and IEEE Xplore conditions before paying anything.

A less rushed broad fallback is [IEEE EIT 2027](https://eit.r4.ieee.org/), whose current full-paper deadline is February 15, 2027.

An IEEE-formatted class paper is not automatically an IEEE publication. Acceptance requires:

- A genuinely novel or unusually rigorous contribution.
- Peer review.
- Correct authorship.
- Registration and usually an author presentation.
- Sufficient funds or institutional support for registration and travel.
- No exaggerated medical claims.

You cannot guarantee publication, but you can build a paper that is actually submission-worthy. Of the three, Choledoch gives you the best “top paper” story - provided you make **evaluation rigor, leakage prevention, and efficiency** the contribution.

## AI assistant | 2026-08-13 01:22:18

You’re right - I overcomplicated the first evaluation.

Based on the orientation example, you should choose an **object-detection dataset with existing bounding-box labels**, preferably ordinary JPG/PNG images. I would no longer recommend hyperspectral Choledoch as your first choice if you are working mostly alone and are still learning the concepts.

## What are we actually looking for?

There are three related tasks:

| Task | Model output |
|---|---|
| Classification | “This image contains a tumor.” |
| Object detection | “There is a tumor here,” with a rectangle around it. |
| Segmentation | Colours the exact pixels belonging to the tumor. |

The liver-tumor example used **object detection**.

You do not personally inspect every image and decide where the disease is. Medical experts have already done that when creating the dataset.

For example, a training image might have a label saying:

```text
Class: polyp
Box: x=240, y=130, width=180, height=160
```

The model sees many images paired with boxes. It learns what visual patterns commonly appear inside boxes labelled “polyp.” On a new image, it might output:

```text
Polyp: 91% confidence
Box: x=235, y=126, width=188, height=165
```

Your application simply draws that rectangle.

The main metric, IoU, asks: **How much does the model’s rectangle overlap with the expert’s rectangle?**

### What would your research investigate?

Your research question would be:

> **Can realistic image augmentation help a lightweight polyp detector maintain its accuracy when tested on images from a hospital it never encountered during training?**

Colonoscopy images can contain:

- Blur caused by camera movement.
- Bright reflections.
- Dark areas.
- Bubbles.
- Compression artifacts.
- Partial obstruction.

You would train:

1. Baseline lightweight detector with normal augmentation.
2. The same detector with realistic medical-image degradations.
3. Possibly one second architecture for comparison.

Then test both on hospital C6.

That is understandable and defensible:

> “We are detecting polyps. We want to know whether a lightweight model continues working when the hospital, camera, and population change.”

### Web application

1. User uploads a colonoscopy JPG.
2. Model finds possible polyps.
3. Application draws boxes.
4. It shows confidence and inference time.
5. If nothing is detected, it clearly says so.

This most closely matches the liver-tumor example you saw.

**Publication potential: 8/10**

### 2. GRAZPEDWRI-DX

**What the model finds:** Fractures in children’s wrist X-rays.

**Input:** Wrist X-ray PNG.

**Output:** Rectangle around a suspected fracture.

**Proposed title:**

> **Patient-Independent Pediatric Wrist Fracture Detection with View-Specific Error Analysis**

The dataset contains:

- 20,327 X-ray images.
- 6,091 patients.
- Boxes and other annotations created by pediatric radiologists.
- Ready-to-use YOLO-format labels.
- 16-bit PNG images.
- Approximately 15.2 GB of data.

It is unusually convenient because it already provides YOLO, Pascal VOC, and other annotation formats. [Official dataset paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9122976/)

### Research question

> **How well does a lightweight fracture detector generalize to completely unseen patients, and does performance differ between front and side X-ray views?**

You would simplify the labels:

- Combine the relevant fracture annotations into one class: `fracture`.
- Ignore more complicated secondary findings for the first version.

Your primary contribution would be splitting by **patient**, not randomly by image. A patient usually has several X-rays; if one enters training and another enters testing, the result may be artificially high.

### Web application

Upload wrist X-ray → model draws a box around suspected fractures.

**Difficulty: 7/10**  
**Publication potential: 7.5/10**  
**Excellent second proposal.**

---

### 3. RSNA Pneumonia Detection Dataset

**What the model finds:** Lung-opacity regions in chest X-rays.

It is important to call the target a **lung opacity**, not automatically a confirmed pneumonia diagnosis. Pneumonia diagnosis normally requires other clinical information.

**Input:** Chest X-ray.

**Output:** Box around potential lung-opacity regions.

**Proposed title:**

> **Effect of Chest X-Ray Preprocessing on Lightweight Lung-Opacity Detection**

The dataset provides:

- Approximately 30,000 chest X-rays.
- Patient identifiers.
- Positive and negative cases.
- Bounding-box coordinates for positive cases.
- Annotations prepared through an RSNA challenge involving expert radiologists. [RSNA challenge](https://www.kaggle.com/c/rsna-pneumonia-detection-challenge/notebooks), [official dataset description](https://www.rsna.org/artificial-intelligence/-/media/Files/RSNA/Education/AI%20resources%20and%20training/AI%20image%20challenge/RSNA-2018-Pneumonia-Detection-Challenge-Dataset-Description.ashx)

### Research question

> **Does medically appropriate contrast normalization improve the detection of lung opacities without increasing false alarms?**

You could compare:

1. Normal grayscale conversion.
2. Standard intensity normalization.
3. CLAHE or another controlled contrast-enhancement method.

### Disadvantage

The original images use DICOM, a medical-image format. They must be carefully converted to PNG without destroying intensity information. That makes it somewhat harder than PolypGen.

**Difficulty: 7.5/10**  
**Publication potential: 6.5/10**  
**Good dataset, but the topic is heavily studied.**

---

## Where Choledoch fits now

The target would be:

> Cancerous cholangiocarcinoma tissue inside a microscopic tissue image.

The annotations identify cancer regions, but these regions are irregular areas rather than neat, separate objects. That makes **segmentation** a more natural task than drawing one rectangle.

The additional difficulties are:

- Every hyperspectral scene contains 60 grayscale images - not one normal image.
- Special `.raw` and `.hdr` formats are involved.
- The original dataset is enormous.
- A normal user cannot easily upload a hyperspectral image through a basic web interface.
- Some annotations may be coarse.
- Converting irregular tumor regions into boxes is possible but scientifically less natural.
- You would first have to understand wavelengths, band selection, false-colour visualisation, and hyperspectral preprocessing.

So my revised verdict is:

> **Choledoch is technically possible, but it is not the sensible first object-detection project for one third-year student who is still learning the workflow.**

It remains an interesting future thesis topic. I would not risk the current 40%-of-grade project on it.

## What makes the PolypGen topic research-worthy?

You do not need to invent an entirely new neural network.

A solid paper can contribute through a better experiment:

```text
Train:
Hospital C1
Hospital C2
Hospital C3
Hospital C4

Validation:
Hospital C5

Final unseen test:
Hospital C6
```

Then compare:

```text
Model A:
Normal training

Model B:
Training with blur, lighting,
reflection and compression augmentation
```

Measure:

- Box mAP.
- Precision: Of all boxes produced, how many were correct?
- Recall: Of all real polyps, how many were found?
- IoU: How closely did predicted boxes overlap expert boxes?
- False positives on images without polyps.
- Inference speed.
- Performance on small versus large polyps.

Your conclusion might be:

> “Artifact-aware augmentation improved recall on the unseen hospital, particularly for small or poorly illuminated polyps, while adding no inference-time cost.”

That is a real, understandable research result.

## The exact three proposals I would give your professor

1. **PolypGen:** Cross-hospital polyp object detection using a lightweight detector and realistic endoscopy-image augmentation.
2. **GRAZPEDWRI-DX:** Patient-independent pediatric wrist-fracture detection with separate analysis of front and side X-ray views.
3. **RSNA Pneumonia Detection:** Lung-opacity detection with a comparison of medical-image contrast-preprocessing strategies.

If non-medical topics are allowed and you want an emergency easy option, replace RSNA with TrashCan underwater debris detection.

My strong personal recommendation is **PolypGen**. It most closely resembles the orientation example, has a clearly defined target, supports boxes and segmentation, uses ordinary images, provides a meaningful unseen-hospital experiment, and remains manageable for one determined student.

## The pattern behind stronger recent IEEE papers

The better papers are rarely just:

> “We trained the newest YOLO model to detect something.”

A stronger paper usually has this structure:

> Important problem + difficult situation + a specific improvement + fair comparison + speed/real-world testing

Recent IEEE computer-vision work repeatedly focuses on:

- Small or partly hidden objects
- Normal-camera plus thermal-camera fusion
- Models that work in new environments, not just their training data
- Limited-label or semi-supervised learning
- Lightweight models for edge devices
- Knowing when a model may be wrong
- Detailed testing under different weather, lighting, distance, and obstruction conditions

You can see these themes throughout the [2025 IEEE TCSVT index](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stampPDF/getPDF.jsp?arnumber=11352539): few-shot detection, multimodal fusion, small-object detection, uncertainty, generalization, distillation, underwater detection, and edge deployment.

A recent wildfire paper is a good example. It did not merely run YOLO on smoke images: it compared three semi-supervised methods, tested real-time performance, and used EigenCAM to check what the model was looking at. [IEEE wildfire-smoke paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11491719/)

The question IEEE reviewers want answered is:

> “What useful thing did we learn that was not already obvious?”

## My three recommended proposals

### 1. Visibility-Aware RGB–Thermal Pedestrian Detection

**Proposed title:**

> Visibility-Aware Late Fusion of RGB and Thermal Images for Pedestrian Detection in Adverse Road Conditions

**What are you detecting?**

People on or near roads. The output is exactly like the orientation example: boxes around each detected person.

Each scene has:

- A normal RGB photograph
- A thermal or “heat camera” image of the same scene

The basic idea is that a normal camera may work better during daylight, while thermal can work better at night, in fog, or when a person is hard to see.

**Dataset: LYNRED-MDS**

This is a particularly attractive dataset because its formal IEEE data paper was published only in May 2026. It contains 4,000 synchronized RGB–thermal pairs covering urban, rural, mountainous, daytime, nighttime, seasonal, and difficult weather conditions. The full detection subset has approximately 80,000 annotations across nine classes. [IEEE LYNRED-MDS paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11533396), [official dataset page](https://www.lynred.com/lynred-mobility-dataset)

**The actual research question:**

> Can a simple system that intelligently chooses how much to trust the normal camera and thermal camera beat either camera by itself?

You would compare:

1. Normal-camera detector only
2. Thermal-camera detector only
3. Simple 50/50 combination
4. Your proposed visibility-aware combination

For example, when the normal image is very dark or its detection confidence is weak, your system gives more importance to thermal detections.

This is called “late fusion,” but it really just means:

> Train two normal detectors, then combine their boxes intelligently.

You do not have to build a giant custom neural network.

**Why it has strong IEEE potential**

- Uses a brand-new IEEE-described dataset
- Fits the current multimodal-AI trend
- Has a clear research question
- Can be tested separately for day, night, occlusion, and temperature
- Produces an impressive visual demonstration
- Fits autonomous-driving and edge-AI research

IEEE IPAS 2027 even has special sessions on autonomous-driving perception and edge AI; its current submission deadline is November 10, 2026, after your October project deadline. [IEEE IPAS 2027](https://events.vtools.ieee.org/m/563249)

**Difficulty:** 7/10  
**Publication ceiling:** 9/10  
**Solo risk:** Medium

One important restriction: the LYNRED license permits research and educational use but prohibits publicly distributing trained weights. You can report results and demonstrate locally, but should not upload the final trained model publicly without permission. [LYNRED license](https://www.lynred.com/sites/default/files/2025-05/LYNRED-Mobility-Dataset-License.pdf)

---

### 2. Detecting People Hidden by Trees Using a Thermal Drone

**Proposed title:**

> Occlusion- and Altitude-Robust Thermal Person Detection for UAV Search and Rescue

**What are you detecting?**

Missing or injured people viewed from a drone, especially people partly hidden behind trees and vegetation.

The system draws a box around each suspected person.

This is my recommended choice if you are genuinely doing most of the work alone.

**Dataset: POP**

The 2025 POP dataset contains:

- 8,768 thermal drone images
- 25,811 person boxes
- Official training, validation, and test sets
- Drone heights of 30, 50, and 70 metres
- Sunny, cloudy, overcast, and foggy conditions
- People lying down or partly hidden by vegetation
- Ready conversion to YOLO format

The dataset is unrestricted for research use. [POP dataset paper in Scientific Data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-04600-0)

The original study found a clear weakness: performance drops significantly when more than about 70% of the person is hidden.

**The actual research question:**

> Can targeted training augmentations help a small detector find people who are more heavily hidden or farther away?

In simple terms, you deliberately make some training images harder:

- Partly cover people with vegetation-like patches
- Make people appear smaller
- Alter thermal contrast
- Add light blur or noise

Then compare:

1. Normal lightweight detector
2. Detector with ordinary augmentation
3. Detector with your targeted “hidden-person” augmentation

Report results separately at 30 m, 50 m, and 70 m - not only one overall score.

That detailed breakdown is what turns the project into research. You might discover, for example:

> “Our method improves recall at 70 metres but provides little benefit at 30 metres.”

Even a result like that is publishable knowledge if the experiment is rigorous.

**Why it has strong IEEE potential**

- Search and rescue is socially important
- One simple class: person
- Tiny-object and occlusion problems are current IEEE themes
- Straightforward bounding-box demo
- Training is much easier than hyperspectral medical imaging
- You can measure accuracy, speed, and model size
- Suitable for a lightweight or edge-AI paper

The recent IEEE literature strongly emphasizes tiny-object detection, including newly published work specifically studying why tiny targets are ignored by detectors. [IEEE TPAMI tiny-object paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11251201)

**Difficulty:** 5/10  
**Publication ceiling:** 8/10  
**Solo suitability:** Excellent

The important warning is that simply comparing YOLO versions would repeat the dataset paper. Your contribution needs to be the targeted training strategy, altitude analysis, and ideally one external-dataset test.

---

### 3. Solar-Panel Hotspot Detection That Works Across Different Thermal Color Palettes

**Proposed title:**

> Palette-Robust Solar Panel Hotspot Detection from Radiometric Thermal Images

**What are you detecting?**

Abnormally hot areas on solar panels. The system draws boxes around possible hotspots.

A thermal camera can display the same heat information using different color themes:

- Grayscale
- Red/yellow heat map
- Rainbow
- Iron-style palette

The problem is that an AI model may accidentally memorize the colors instead of learning the actual hotspot pattern.

**Dataset: PV-HSD-2025**

The dataset contains:

- 4,025 thermal defect images
- 25,181 hotspot boxes
- 16-bit thermal R-JPEG data
- 512×640 resolution
- YOLO-format labels
- Support for multiple palette renderings

[PV-HSD-2025 dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MisakaMikoto128/PV-HSD-2025), [dataset manuscript](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/3b839bb0-23f5-4b41-b0fe-dd84e2e7029f-MECA.pdf?abstractid=5134282&mirid=1)

**The actual research question:**

> Does the model learn the hotspot itself, or does it merely memorize the thermal color palette?

You would render the same raw thermal images using several palettes and compare:

1. Train on grayscale, test on grayscale
2. Train on grayscale, test on an unseen colored palette
3. Train using several randomized palettes
4. Train using normalized raw thermal values

The proposed result would be a model that remains accurate even when the thermal camera’s display palette changes.

This is much stronger than generic solar hotspot detection, because IEEE has already published the straightforward “YOLO detects solar hotspots” version. [Existing IEEE solar-hotspot paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10576312/)

**Why it has strong IEEE potential**

- Renewable-energy application
- Sensor-aware research question
- Easy-to-understand visual result
- Controlled experiment: same image, different visual appearance
- Tests genuine robustness rather than chasing a slightly higher accuracy
- Uses recent radiometric thermal data

**Difficulty:** 6.5/10  
**Publication ceiling:** 8.5/10  
**Solo risk:** Medium

Before selecting it, confirm the dataset terms with the authors. Its Hugging Face metadata says Apache 2.0, while the written card also mentions academic-only use. That ambiguity should be resolved before publication.

## Best practical non-medical proposal

### Clutter-Aware Instance Segmentation of Construction and Demolition Waste

**Dataset:** [ReCoDeWaste](https://github.com/prasadvineetv/ReCoDeWaste)

**What the system sees:** Piles or conveyor scenes containing overlapping construction waste.

**What it produces:** A colored outline or mask around every individual object, classified as:

- Aggregate
- Cardboard
- Hard plastic
- Metal
- Soft plastic
- Timber

The 2025 dataset has 2,505 high-resolution RGB-depth image pairs and more than 100,000 manually annotated object masks. [Dataset paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0956053X25005343)

You can initially use only the normal RGB images, so you do not need to develop an RGB-depth fusion model.

**Research question:**

> How much does clutter and object overlap reduce the assigned model’s ability to separate recyclable construction materials?

You can calculate a clutter level for every image:

- Low clutter: few objects
- Medium clutter: moderate number of objects
- High clutter: many touching or overlapping objects

Then compare:

1. Baseline training
2. Training with crop, occlusion, and object-overlap augmentation
3. Performance for low-, medium-, and high-clutter scenes
4. Per-material performance
5. Speed and model size

If your professor assigns object detection instead of instance segmentation, the existing masks can be converted into bounding boxes. Therefore, the dataset works for either task.

**Why I like it**

- Much less ordinary than road-damage detection
- Dataset was released with a 2025 research paper
- Six useful classes
- Industrial and environmental relevance
- Visually impressive segmentation output
- Supports a meaningful clutter/occlusion study
- Strong alignment with current recycling automation research

IEEE IPAS 2027 currently has a special session specifically on AI-driven waste sorting and recycling, which makes this direction especially well aligned with a future submission. [IEEE IPAS 2027](https://events.vtools.ieee.org/m/563249)

## 1. Medical: First-aid supply segmentation

Proposed title:

> **Occlusion-Robust Instance Segmentation of First-Aid Supplies in Cluttered Emergency Kits**

What the application does:

You upload a photograph of a first-aid kit. The model colors and outlines every medical supply it recognizes.

Possible classes:

- Bandage roll
- Gauze pack
- Medicine bottle
- Needleless syringe
- Medical mask

Example idea:

```text
Photo of messy kit
        ↓
Colored outline around every syringe, bandage and gauze pack
        ↓
Item count and confidence
```

Why this is a better medical project than tumor segmentation:

- You can personally tell where an object begins and ends.
- You do not need a radiologist or pathologist.
- You are not claiming to diagnose somebody.
- You control the photography and dataset quality.
- Objects can be demonstrated live during the presentation.
- The masks have clear physical boundaries.

The research question should not simply be “Can the model recognize supplies?” Instead:

> How much do clutter, low lighting and partial covering affect first-aid supply segmentation, and can condition-specific augmentation improve robustness?

Dataset design:

- Approximately 700–1,000 raw photographs
- Four or five classes
- Multiple physical examples of every class
- Clean, cluttered, partially covered and low-light scenes
- Different tables, bags and backgrounds
- Approximately 1,500–2,500 total object masks

Important testing rule:

Do not place photographs of the exact same physical object in training and testing. For example, if one specific medicine bottle is in training, use a different bottle design in the final test set. Otherwise, the model can memorize that particular object.

Verdict: **Best medical proposal for you.**

It is medical enough to match the professor’s previous projects, but it avoids the enormous risk of labeling tumors incorrectly. Surgical-instrument segmentation is an active IEEE research area, showing that segmentation of medical equipment is a legitimate research direction - not everything medical needs to diagnose disease. See recent work on [surgical-instrument segmentation using foundation models](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10807204/) and [real-time segmentation in laparoscopic surgery](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10552879).

## 2. Other: Electronic-waste segmentation

Proposed title:

> **Clutter-Aware Instance Segmentation of Electronic Waste for Small-Scale Automated Sorting**

What the application does:

You photograph a pile of discarded electronics. The system precisely outlines each battery, circuit board, phone or power adapter.

Recommended classes:

- Battery
- Circuit board
- Mobile phone
- Power adapter
- Cable, only if you are willing to outline a difficult thin object

Why it is strong:

- Sustainability and automated recycling are active research areas.
- E-waste is more specialized than ordinary road damage or generic trash.
- Objects can overlap, which creates a real segmentation challenge.
- You can obtain data from old household electronics or, with permission, a repair shop.
- It can become a genuinely new public dataset.
- No medical expert or specialized imaging equipment is required.

Strong research question:

> How does object overlap affect electronic-waste segmentation, and can occlusion-focused data augmentation improve the segmentation of partially visible components?

Recommended experiment:

Train the prescribed model normally, then test it under three conditions:

1. Separated objects
2. Lightly cluttered objects
3. Heavily overlapping objects

Report the mask mAP and IoU separately for each condition. This is much more paper-like than reporting only one overall score.

Dataset design:

- Approximately 700–1,200 photographs
- Four primary classes
- Different physical models and brands
- Clean and cluttered arrangements
- Different lighting and backgrounds
- Test objects that were never photographed during training

Safety: do not open, puncture or manipulate swollen lithium batteries.

Verdict: **My best overall recommendation.**

It is the best balance of originality, manageable annotation and IEEE potential.

A public fallback is the [raw HDPE recyclable-waste image collection](https://zenodo.org/records/11504453). Its repository lists one raw RGB/HSI archive, no supplied segmentation files, and a CC BY 4.0 license. However, it apparently contains only HDPE recyclable objects, so your segmentation would probably be one-class and less distinctive than a new e-waste dataset.

- Cup or can

Research question:

> How do water reflections, glare, partial submersion and small object size affect floating-litter segmentation?

Why it could be impressive:

- The masks look excellent in a demo.
- It connects AI with water pollution and environmental monitoring.
- Reflections and partial submersion create a meaningful technical challenge.
- Locally collected Philippine waterway images would provide geographical novelty.
- It could eventually support cleanup boats or environmental monitoring.

Why it is harder:

- Some litter will be tiny.
- Water reflections can resemble objects.
- Part of an object may be underwater.
- Flexible plastic has difficult boundaries.
- You need several locations and days for credible testing.
- You must collect imagery safely and avoid including identifiable people.

Dataset plan:

- 500–900 images or sampled video frames
- At least 10–15 independent video clips
- Several waterways or controlled water environments
- Split the dataset by entire video/location
- Never randomly distribute adjacent video frames across training and testing

A public fallback exists: the FloW creators provide [200 explicitly unannotated floating-waste video sequences](https://orca-tech.cn/datasets/FloW/FloW-Img). But there are two concerns:

- The same project also contains a labeled image subset.
- The download terms/license are not clearly shown on the public page.

Therefore, I would only propose FloW after showing the page to your professor and confirming that an unannotated subset of a larger collection is acceptable.

Verdict: **Highest “wow factor,” but also the hardest option for one active member.**

# Why I removed the dental and tumor options

DENTEX does contain [1,571 explicitly unlabeled panoramic dental X-rays](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/DENTEX/blob/main/README.md), but segmentation makes it impractical for you:

- Every image can contain around 20–32 teeth.
- Each tooth needs an accurate individual mask.
- Just 500 images could require roughly 12,000–15,000 masks.
- Teeth overlap in panoramic images.
- Determining abnormal regions requires dental expertise.
- Recent tooth-segmentation research is already technically advanced, making a basic model comparison difficult to publish.

The Microscopic Hyperspectral Choledoch dataset is even less suitable now. Tumor boundaries would require a pathologist, hyperspectral files add considerable technical complexity, and incorrect masks would invalidate the results.

So my medical recommendation is now **medical-supply segmentation**, not tumor, tooth or organ segmentation.

# What recent publishable segmentation work tends to do

The recurring pattern is:

1. Use or introduce a specialized dataset.
2. Focus on one difficult real-world condition.
3. Evaluate boundary/mask quality carefully.
4. Test on a genuinely different site, session or object set.
5. Include failure cases - not only successful examples.
6. Discuss accuracy together with inference speed and deployment.

Recent IEEE/CVF work emphasizes annotation efficiency, robustness and boundary quality. For example, [SegBuilder at WACV 2025](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/WACV2025/html/Reza_SegBuilder_A_Semi-Automatic_Annotation_Tool_for_Segmentation_WACV_2025_paper.html) used human-verified SAM suggestions to accelerate mask creation. Recent medical segmentation research also focuses heavily on reducing annotation requirements through [efficient prompting and human feedback](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/html/Konwer_Enhancing_SAM_with_Efficient_Prompting_and_Preference_Optimization_for_Semi-supervised_CVPR_2025_paper.html).

That means your strongest contribution is probably:

> A new raw dataset + carefully verified masks + controlled robustness testing.

It does not need to be a brand-new neural-network architecture.

# Annotation warning

Segmentation is much more time-consuming than drawing boxes. For every object, you need to trace its shape.

For one active student, I would limit the accepted project to:

- 4 classes maximum initially
- 600–1,000 images
- Around 1,200–2,500 total object masks
- Clear, physical objects
- No tumors, diseases or fuzzy biological regions
- Human verification of every mask

You may use a SAM-assisted tool to suggest an outline, but correct it manually. Ask the professor whether assisted annotation is permitted and document exactly how every mask was checked.

# My final ranking

1. **E-waste instance segmentation**  -  best overall and best publication balance.
2. **First-aid supply instance segmentation**  -  safest medical proposal.
3. **Floating-litter instance segmentation**  -  most exciting, but substantially harder.

These are also intentionally model-independent. If your professor later prescribes YOLO, Mask R-CNN or another model, the dataset and research questions remain valid.

For your project, the downloaded images/videos should have:

- no bounding boxes;
- no segmentation masks;
- no class labels;
- no CSV/XML/JSON annotation files;
- no filenames or folders revealing the correct class;
- no ready-made train/validation split based on labels.

## 1. HDPE recyclable-object segmentation  -  safest option

**Dataset:** [Raw RGB and hyperspectral HDPE waste images](https://zenodo.org/records/11504453)

The dataset shows plastic objects moving on a conveyor belt. You would use only the ordinary RGB images.

### What the AI does

It draws a precise mask around every separate plastic object:

- object 1 = one mask;
- object 2 = another mask;
- conveyor/background = no mask.

This is instance segmentation, not merely drawing a box.

### Proposed title

**Instance Segmentation of Overlapping HDPE Recyclables in Conveyor-Belt Images**

### Why it is strong

- Objects have understandable boundaries.
- No medical knowledge is required.
- The dataset is only around 830 MB.
- Overlapping, translucent and partially hidden plastic creates a legitimate research problem.
- The source provides raw RGB and hyperspectral data under CC BY 4.0.

### Possible paper contribution

Compare performance under:

- isolated versus overlapping objects;
- clear versus motion-blurred objects;
- lightly versus heavily cluttered scenes.

This is probably your safest solo project.

## 2. Surgical instrument segmentation  -  best medical option

**Dataset:** [Hamlyn Centre Laparoscopic/Endoscopic Video Datasets](https://hamlyn.doc.ic.ac.uk/vision/)

Use selected raw porcine surgery videos showing instruments interacting with tissue.

### What the AI does

For each frame, it colors the exact pixels occupied by each surgical instrument.

You are **not diagnosing cancer or identifying diseases**. You only identify a clearly visible physical object: the instrument.

### Proposed title

**Robust Instance Segmentation of Surgical Instruments under Smoke, Glare, and Occlusion**

### Why it is strong

- Medical topic without needing a doctor to decide whether tissue is diseased.
- Instruments are visually recognizable.
- Difficult conditions create a publishable problem:
  - smoke;
  - blood;
  - specular glare;
  - motion blur;
  - instruments partly hidden by tissue.
- Video results make an impressive presentation.

### Important rule

Split the dataset by **entire video**, not by random frames. Otherwise, nearly identical frames can appear in training and testing, making the result look artificially excellent.

### Eligibility risk

Some Hamlyn collections include other types of ground truth. You must identify the exact raw video files you intend to use and confirm that an unannotated sequence is acceptable.

## 3. Mixed-traffic vehicle segmentation  -  best “interesting” option

**Dataset:** [Visaitech Vehicle Mixed Traffic Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/visaitech/vehicle-mixed-traffic-detection)

This contains 203 unannotated dashcam video clips from dense South Asian traffic.

### What the AI does

It creates separate masks for road users such as:

- motorcycles;
- three-wheelers;
- cars/other four-wheelers.

For a solo project, I recommend only **two-wheelers and three-wheelers**. Do not begin with every possible vehicle class.

### Proposed title

**Instance Segmentation of Two- and Three-Wheeled Vehicles in Dense Mixed-Traffic Videos**

### Why it is strong

- Similar traffic conditions exist in the Philippines.
- Motorcycles and three-wheelers are frequently crowded and partially hidden.
- Most popular datasets focus heavily on cars in more orderly road environments.
- It has a good smart-city and road-safety application.
- The raw archive has approximately 12 GB of unannotated video.

### Eligibility risk

The raw videos are unannotated, but the same project also releases box annotations for a small, separate collection of frames. There are no segmentation masks, but your professor may still reject the repository if the rule applies to the entire project.

## AI assistant | 2026-08-17 15:50:58

Yes, your professor is right.

A box says, “the object is somewhere inside this rectangle.” Segmentation says, “these exact pixels belong to the object.”

One important question remains:

- **Semantic segmentation:** all pixels belonging to “chicken” receive one combined mask.
- **Instance segmentation:** every individual chicken receives a separate mask.

Because the previous projects used YOLO segmentation and said “instance segmentation,” you are probably doing the second one.

## 1. Free-range chicken instance segmentation

**Dataset:** [Raw Chicken Gender Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/hongxun/raw-data-chicken-gender)

A recent survey reports that it contains **4,272 unannotated high-resolution images**, with several free-moving chickens appearing indoors and outdoors. The images are approximately 3072×4080 pixels. [Dataset survey](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11762189/)

### Proposed title

**Instance Segmentation of Free-Range Chickens under Occlusion and Varying Farm Conditions**

### What you label

Every visible chicken receives its own pixel mask. You do not identify gender, breed, disease or behavior.

### Why this is strong

- Raw images reportedly have no annotations.
- Clear real-world application: automated livestock counting and monitoring.
- Crowding, shadows and overlapping chickens create a legitimate challenge.
- Less overused than cars, road damage or plant disease.
- Easy for an audience to understand.

### Research question

> How does chicken density and inter-animal occlusion affect instance-segmentation accuracy?

You could manually classify the test images into:

- low crowding;
- medium crowding;
- high crowding.

These are your own experimental conditions, not source labels.

### Workload

Approximately 400–600 images and 2,000–4,000 chicken masks. This is heavier than HDPE but still realistic with annotation assistance.

This is one of my favorite new options for you.

## 2. Red blood cell instance segmentation

**Dataset:** [ThalassemiaPBS](https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/gd9ysj73jd/1)

This is a raw peripheral-blood-smear dataset from four thalassemia patients, released under CC BY 4.0. The dataset has approximately 80 microscope images.

### Proposed title

**Instance Segmentation of Overlapping Red Blood Cells in Unannotated Peripheral Blood Smear Images**

### What you label

Every visible red blood cell gets a separate mask.

You are not deciding whether a cell is diseased. You are only separating visible cells from the background and from each other.

### Why it is interesting

- Genuine medical application.
- No tumor diagnosis or medical classification.
- Cells are mostly visually recognizable.
- Overlapping and irregularly shaped cells provide a real segmentation challenge.
- Even though there are only around 80 images, each image may contain dozens of cells.

Research using comparable blood-smear images found that 50 annotated images containing roughly 44 cells each could provide a reasonable starting point for training an RBC segmentation model. [RedTell study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2023.1058720/full)

### Main weakness

The images come from only four patients. You would ideally split them by patient, but that may be impossible if patient group information was removed. This limitation must be honestly discussed in the paper.

### Verdict

Best medical option if your professor rejects unannotated subsets from larger, partly annotated repositories.

Separate pixel masks for each visible surgical instrument.

## 4. Capsule-endoscopy visual-obstruction segmentation

### Proposed title

**Pixel-Level Segmentation of Visual Obstructions in Unlabeled Capsule-Endoscopy Images**

### What you label

Rather than disease, outline regions where the camera view is blocked by:

- food or intestinal debris;
- heavily obscured areas.

This would probably be semantic segmentation because all obstructed pixels can share one mask.

### Risk

You need a very clear annotation rule. For example:

Without such a rule, two annotators may disagree about which pixels are “obstructed.”

## AI assistant | 2026-08-18 22:19:08

This is a technically interesting dataset, but **FPIC is not eligible under your professor’s “absolutely no labels or metadata” rule**.

## Why FPIC fails the rule

The official page describes FPIC as:

- 261 high-resolution images;
- 93 physical PCBs;
- more than 71,000 annotated component/text instances;
- precise polygon contours around components;
- metadata identifying text, logos and component designators;
- scale, color-calibration and camera information;
- descriptions of many PCB samples.

The accompanying paper explicitly says FPIC provides “labeled ground truth,” semantic component boundaries and component-to-silkscreen relationships. [Official FPIC page](https://physicaldb.ece.ufl.edu/index.php/fics-pcb-image-collection-fpic/) and [FPIC paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08414).

Its download is separated into:

- `pcb_image.zip`  -  PNG images;
- `smd_annotation.zip`  -  CSV polygon annotations.

Those CSV contours can already be converted directly into segmentation masks. [Existing FPIC processing code](https://github.com/CandleLabAI/PCBSegClassNet)

Therefore, downloading only `pcb_image.zip` does not change the fact that you selected an already-annotated segmentation dataset.

## Is the research idea itself good?

Yes. PCB component segmentation is a strong industrial-computer-vision topic:

> The model precisely colors every electronic component on a circuit board instead of only placing rectangles around them.

Possible output:

- separate mask for every integrated circuit;
- separate mask for every capacitor;
- separate mask for every connector;
- PCB/background left uncolored.

But using FPIC ordinarily would not be very novel. PCB segmentation has already been studied heavily on it.

For example, **PCBSegClassNet** used FPIC for PCB component segmentation and reported:

- 96.3% Dice;
- 92.7% IoU;
- 25 component classes;
- 19,158 extracted component images.

[Published PCBSegClassNet results](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0957417423005316)

Other research has already compared U-Net, SAM and Detectron2 on FPIC, with reported IoU reaching around 93.95%. [University of Kansas project](https://eecs.ku.edu/triad-approaches-pcb-component-segmentation-and-classification-using-u-net-sam-and-detectron2)

Simply training your assigned YOLO segmentation model on FPIC would mostly reproduce existing work.

## Another hidden problem: data leakage

“261 images” does not mean 261 independent boards. There are only 93 physical PCBs, and some were photographed multiple times under different camera settings.

If one photo of a board enters training and another photo of the same board enters testing, the model may memorize its layout. The FPIC authors explicitly warn about treating transformed photographs of the same PCB as unseen samples.

A proper study must split by **physical PCB identity**, not randomly by image. Unfortunately, PCB identity is metadata - which your professor also prohibits.

|---|---:|
| Interesting application | 9/10 |
| Good segmentation target | 9/10 |
| Eligible under professor’s rule | **0/10** |
| Novelty using FPIC + ordinary YOLO segmentation | 3/10 |
| Solo feasibility | 5/10 |
| IEEE potential if you create new PCB data | 8/10 |

I would **not spend one of your three proposal slots on FPIC** unless your professor explicitly answers yes to:

> “FPIC distributes its raw PNG images separately from its annotation CSV files. May we use only the PNG archive and create completely new masks, even though annotations exist separately?”

Given the words “absolutely no labels or metadata,” I expect the answer to be no.

## A better PCB version

If you genuinely like PCBs, the stronger proposal would be:

### Proposed title

**Instance Segmentation of Integrated Circuits in Uncontrolled Electronic-Waste PCB Images**

### What the model identifies

Every visible integrated-circuit chip receives its own pixel-level mask.

Use only one class initially:

- `integrated circuit`

Do not attempt 25 component types. Even the FPIC authors note that capacitors, inductors, thermistors and ferrite beads can look extremely similar to nonexperts.

### Data collection

Photograph discarded PCBs from:

- broken computers;
- routers;
- televisions;
- computer repair shops;
- university electronics laboratories;
- e-waste facilities.

Aim for:

- 50–100 genuinely different PCBs;
- front and back when appropriate;
- 500–800 final images;
- different lighting, angles and backgrounds;
- approximately 2,000–4,000 IC masks;
- no class folders or meaningful filenames;
- EXIF removed if required.

### Research question

> How robustly can an instance-segmentation model isolate integrated circuits from electronic-waste PCBs under changes in board color, component density, viewing angle and illumination?

That version is much more publishable because your contribution becomes:

1. a new pixel-level PCB dataset;
2. images from realistic uncontrolled conditions;
3. evaluation on completely unseen circuit boards;
4. an application to automated e-waste recovery.

It precisely colors the pixels belonging to a mobile phone held by a driver.

You can determine “possible distraction” afterward based on whether a phone is segmented near the driver’s hand.

You can combine copied images into one folder for convenience, but **you cannot claim that this makes the original dataset unlabeled**. The original class folders are documented publicly, so deleting them only hides the labels - it does not change the dataset’s provenance.
```text
original_dataset/
  Safe Driving/
  Texting Phone/
  Talking Phones/

working_dataset/
  images/
    img_0001.jpg
    img_0002.jpg
  masks/           ← created entirely by your team
    img_0001.png
    img_0002.png
```

Also rename copied files if their filenames reveal their original class - but document that process. Don’t remove embedded metadata merely to disguise the source.

The important distinction is:

- Folder names = only tell you what activity is happening in the whole picture.
- Bounding boxes = tell you the phone’s rough location.
- Segmentation masks = identify the exact phone pixels.

Your dataset has the first kind, but your research requires the third kind. Therefore, your team is still doing original segmentation annotation.

However, if your professor literally means **“the source must never have had any labels whatsoever,”** flattening the folders will not qualify. You should ask this exact question:

## Avoid another rejection

Submit the **exact unlabeled component**, not merely the overall collection. For example:

> “OpenUrine Unlabeled Subset: 5,640 images with no annotations or patient metadata.”

Do not write only “OpenUrine Dataset,” because the complete collection also includes 790 images with bounding boxes.

Likewise, say:

> “HyperKvasir Unlabeled Image Archive containing 99,417 images.”

The complete HyperKvasir collection also has labeled and segmented components.

Before resubmitting, get one clarification from the professor:

> “Does an officially separated unlabeled subset qualify when the dataset publisher also releases a different labeled subset, or must the entire source collection have never contained annotations?”

If the entire source must have no annotations anywhere, choose **GastroNet-5M**. It is the cleanest match I found.

## My final three recommendations

### 1. Fetal skull segmentation  -  best paper potential

Suggested title:

> **Deep Learning–Based Fetal Skull Segmentation in Routine Ultrasound Images**

You would select only images classified as fetal brain and draw around the bright skull boundary. The clinical story is that accurate skull segmentation could support automated fetal measurements.

### 2. Shoulder implant segmentation  -  easiest unusual topic

Suggested title:

The metal implant is extremely bright and easy to distinguish. It is also much less overused than tumors, blood cells and skin cancer. The smaller 597-image dataset is still workable if you annotate approximately 400–500 images and use transfer learning.

### 3. Cervical-cell segmentation  -  safest standard medical proposal

Suggested title:

> **Joint Nucleus–Cytoplasm Segmentation of Cervical Cells in Pap-Smear Microscopy**

Most images contain one centered cell. You can use two segmentation classes:

- Nucleus
- Cytoplasm

It has a clear medical purpose while remaining practical for students.

## Honest rating

- **Feasibility for your class:** **8.5/10**
- **IEEE conference potential as currently described:** **5.5/10**
- **Potential with a strong research design:** **7–7.5/10**

It is highly doable because the fruits and damaged areas are generally visible, the dataset has 3,167 images, and you can annotate a manageable subset. However, simply training YOLO segmentation and reporting accuracy would not be sufficiently novel. IEEE already contains work on [fruit detection and segmentation](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10016600/), [fresh-versus-damaged fruit classification](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10718540/), [tomato defect datasets](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9095778/), and [post-harvest fruit grading](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10367831/).

To push it closer to IEEE quality:

1. Manually create and release a new pixel-level defect-mask dataset.
2. Segment the **actual damaged surface**, not merely the whole fruit.
3. Compare at least three models, such as YOLO-Seg, U-Net/DeepLabV3+, and SegFormer.
4. Test cross-fruit generalization: train on five fruit types and test on the unseen sixth fruit.
5. Calculate the percentage of damaged surface and investigate whether it corresponds to good, medium, and bad quality grades.
6. Report Dice, mIoU, precision, recall, inference speed and results for each fruit.
7. Create one strict annotation guide explaining what counts as rot, bruising, discoloration or normal ripening.

The strongest research angle would be:

> **Cross-Fruit Generalization of Deep Learning Models for Pixel-Level Post-Harvest Surface Defect Segmentation**

That is substantially more publishable than “fruit defect segmentation using YOLO” because the research question becomes whether an AI trained on certain fruits can recognize defects on a fruit it has never seen.

## AI assistant | 2026-09-03 23:49:09

I’ll teach this specifically for your fruit-defect **segmentation** project: what to label, exactly where to click, how to keep everyone consistent, and how to export the polygons for training. I’ll use CVAT as the example because it supports polygons and YOLO segmentation exports.

## AI assistant | 2026-09-03 23:50:23

Yes. For your project, “annotation” means manually drawing a precise outline around every visible damaged area of a fruit.

The Grade 1/2/3 folders are image-level labels. What you still need are pixel-level segmentation annotations:

- Classification: “This entire image is Grade 3.”
- Segmentation: “These exact pixels are the damaged part.”

## 1. Use CVAT

Use [CVAT Online](https://app.cvat.ai/). It is designed for polygon annotation and can export directly for YOLO segmentation.

Create a project with:

- Project name: `Post-Harvest Fruit Defect Segmentation`
- Label: `surface_defect`
- Shape: Polygon
- Label color: something easy to see, such as red

I strongly recommend starting with only one label: `surface_defect`.

Do not immediately create labels such as bruise, rot, mold, cut, and discoloration. Different defects can look similar, so your group may label them inconsistently.

## 2. Decide what counts as a defect

Draw polygons around:

- Rotten areas
- Bruises
- Cracks, cuts, and punctures
- Mold
- Clearly damaged or unusually discolored areas
- Missing or severely deteriorated fruit tissue

Do not draw polygons around:

- The entire fruit
- The background
- Normal fruit color
- Natural ripening gradients
- Stems and leaves
- Shadows
- Light reflections
- Stickers
- Marks that are too unclear to judge

For an unclear area, do not guess. Flag or skip the image so your group can review it together.

## 3. How to draw one annotation

In CVAT:

1. Create a task and upload around 30–50 practice images.
2. Open the annotation job.
3. Select **Polygon**.
4. Select the `surface_defect` label.
5. Click **Shape**.
6. Zoom in on the damaged area.
7. Click points along the edge of the defect.
8. Add more points where the boundary curves or changes direction.
9. Press `N` or click **Done** to finish the polygon.
10. Drag individual points if the outline needs correction.
11. Press `Ctrl+S` regularly.

CVAT provides an official [polygon annotation guide](https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/annotation/manual-annotation/shapes/annotation-with-polygons/).

Your polygon should look approximately like this:

```text
        Fruit
     ___________
   /             \
  |    xxxxx      |
  |   x     x     |  ← polygon follows only this damaged patch
  |    xxxxx      |
  |         xxx   |  ← second patch gets a separate polygon
   \_____________/
```

Do not create one huge polygon around both areas unless the defects physically connect.

## 4. Important annotation cases

| Situation | What you should do |
|---|---|
| Two separate damaged areas | Draw two polygons |
| One continuous damaged area | Draw one polygon |
| Defect reaches image edge | Outline only the visible portion |
| Healthy fruit | Leave the image empty - no polygon |
| Fuzzy defect boundary | Consistently trace the middle of the transition |
| Shadow or reflection | Do not annotate |
| Tiny but clearly visible defect | Annotate it |
| Defect is impossible to identify | Flag or exclude the image |

Empty healthy images are important. They teach the model that not every dark or differently colored area is damage.

## 5. How precise should the polygon be?

You do not need to click around every single pixel.

A good polygon:

- Stays close to the defect boundary
- Uses additional points around curves
- Does not include large healthy areas
- Does not cross over itself
- Usually has roughly 10–40 points, depending on shape complexity

Your images are only around `224×224`, so some boundaries may genuinely be unclear. Zooming makes pixels larger, but it does not reveal additional detail. Never invent a boundary that cannot be seen.

## 6. Conduct a practice round first

Before annotating hundreds of images:

1. Have every member annotate the same 20 images.
2. Compare the results.
3. Discuss where your polygons disagree.
4. Finalize one written annotation rulebook.
5. Annotate another shared batch of 20 images.
6. Only begin the complete dataset when everyone is consistent.

Example rule:

> A surface defect is a clearly visible localized area showing physical damage, decay, bruising, cracking, mold, or abnormal deterioration. Shadows, reflections, stems, natural color variation, and uncertain marks are excluded.

This consistency is more important than drawing extremely detailed polygons.

## 7. What to do with Grade 1, 2, and 3

Keep those folders because they may be useful for balancing your images:

- Grade 1: mostly healthy/negative examples
- Grade 2: moderate defects
- Grade 3: severe defects

However, your polygon label remains `surface_defect`.

Do not rename the polygons `Grade 1`, `Grade 2`, or `Grade 3`. A grade describes the whole fruit; a defect polygon describes a specific area.

The dataset contains at least 300 images when grades are pooled across fruit types, but several individual fruit-grade combinations have fewer than 300. Therefore, phrase your dataset classes as the three pooled grades unless your professor explicitly demands 300 images for every fruit-and-grade combination.

## 8. Recommended workload

Start with a pilot of 50 images. For the actual study, a manageable initial target is:

- 300 Grade 1 images
- 300 Grade 2 images
- 300 Grade 3 images
- 900 images total

Distribute the six fruit types as evenly as the dataset permits.

Remember: Grade 1 images may contain no defect polygon. That is valid. You should also verify that at least 300 of your selected images actually contain visible, annotatable defects.

## 9. Exporting for training

After reviewing the annotations:

1. Open the CVAT task.
2. Select **Actions → Export task dataset**.
3. Choose **Ultralytics YOLO Segmentation 1.0**.
4. Download and preserve the ZIP file.
5. Also retain a CVAT or COCO backup if possible.

CVAT officially supports exporting polygons and masks in [Ultralytics YOLO Segmentation format](https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/manual/advanced/formats/format-yolo-ultralytics/).

Be careful not to choose ordinary **YOLO Detection**. Detection uses rectangular boxes; your project requires segmentation polygons.

## Final quality checklist

Before approving every image, ask:

- Did I outline every clearly visible defect?
- Is the polygon tight around the damaged area?
- Did I accidentally include healthy fruit?
- Did I mistake a shadow or reflection for damage?
- Are disconnected defects separate polygons?
- Is the label exactly `surface_defect`?
- Did I save the annotation?

Start by annotating only 10 images. You can send me screenshots of two or three completed annotations, and I can tell you whether your boundaries and labeling rules are correct before your team handles hundreds.

## User | 2026-09-03 23:52:33

so what should i look for? 


## AI assistant | 2026-09-03 23:52:42

You should look for **visible damage on the fruit’s surface** - areas that look physically unhealthy compared with the surrounding skin.

Annotate these:

- **Rot:** dark, brown, black, mushy-looking, or decaying patches
- **Bruises:** localized dark or discolored patches
- **Mold:** fuzzy white, gray, green, or black growth
- **Cracks and cuts:** broken or split skin
- **Punctures or holes:** visible physical damage
- **Scars/lesions:** rough, sunken, or abnormal spots
- **Severe discoloration:** only when it clearly looks like damage

Do not annotate these:

- Normal fruit color or ripeness
- The whole fruit
- Stems, leaves, and flower ends
- Shadows
- Camera glare or shiny reflections
- Background objects
- Tiny dots that appear to be normal texture
- Anything you are genuinely unsure about

The easiest rule is:

> If the suspicious patch looks damaged and is visibly different from the healthy skin surrounding it, outline it. If it could simply be normal color, texture, shadow, or lighting, do not outline it.

For example:

- Apple with two brown rotten patches → draw **two polygons**
- Banana with normal yellow and brown ripening spots → probably **do not annotate**
- Banana with a large black, sunken damaged section → **annotate it**
- Mango with a bright white reflection → **do not annotate**
- Papaya with a visible cut → outline the **cut/damaged tissue**, not the entire papaya
- Completely healthy fruit → leave the image **empty**

Your label should simply be:

```text
surface_defect
```

Since distinguishing “bruise” from “rot” can be unreliable from a photograph, put all definite damage under that one label. The most important thing is for every group member to apply the same rule.

## The simplest decision rule

Ask these questions in order:

1. Is it located on the fruit rather than the background?
2. Is it clearly physical damage, decay, mold, a cut, or a localized abnormal patch?
3. Can I see a reasonable boundary around it?
4. Is it definitely not lighting, shadow, normal color, stem, or natural texture?

If all four answers are **yes**, draw a polygon. Otherwise, leave it unannotated or flag it for review.

One warning: the existing Grade 1/2/3 folders were not created specifically as pixel-level defect categories. Do not blindly assume that everything in Grade 2 or Grade 3 must receive a polygon. Annotate only damage that is actually visible.

## Best option for your group

### Ultralytics Platform + SAM Smart Annotation

This is probably the easiest option:

1. Upload the images.
2. Create the class `surface_defect`.
3. Enter **Smart** mode.
4. Click inside a damaged patch.
5. SAM generates the pixel-level mask.
6. Add correction clicks if necessary.
7. Accept the mask and move to the next image.

Ultralytics currently offers SAM 2.1 and SAM 3 in its annotation interface. SAM generates a mask after a click, and additional positive or negative clicks can correct it. The annotations can be used directly for YOLO segmentation. [Ultralytics annotation documentation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/platform/data/annotation)

For example:

- Click inside a dark rotten patch → AI outlines it.
- If it includes healthy fruit → use a negative/subtraction click on the healthy area.
- If it misses part of the defect → use another positive/addition click there.
- Press Enter to save.

This is much faster than manually placing 30 polygon points.

## Second-best option: CVAT with SAM

CVAT also supports AI-assisted polygon creation:

1. Click the magic-wand tool.
2. Select `surface_defect`.
3. Select a SAM/interactor model.
4. Left-click inside the defect.
5. Right-click areas that should not be included.
6. Convert the generated mask to a polygon if required.
7. Correct and save it.

CVAT explicitly supports positive and negative points and can convert returned masks into editable polygons. [CVAT AI Interactor instructions](https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/annotation/auto-annotation/ai-tools/)

The catch is that SAM availability depends on the CVAT installation. CVAT Online and self-hosted versions support different model-deployment methods. [CVAT AI model documentation](https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/annotation/auto-annotation/ai-models/)

## Other available choices

| Tool | What the AI does | My recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Ultralytics Platform** | Click-based masks using SAM 2.1 or SAM 3 | **Best/easiest** |
| **CVAT + SAM** | Positive/negative clicks produce editable masks or polygons | Best if already using CVAT |
| **Roboflow Smart Polygon** | A few clicks generate a SAM polygon | Also beginner-friendly |
| **Local SAM 2/3 pipeline** | Runs segmentation on your own PC | Best if privacy/control matters |
| **Label Studio + SAM** | Interactive SAM masks | More complicated; its documented SAM setup has export limitations |

Roboflow’s official documentation confirms that Smart Polygon and SAM Label Assist create polygon annotations using a few clicks. [Roboflow Annotate documentation](https://docs.roboflow.com/annotate)

## Can Codex do it?

Codex can help build a local system that:

- Loads every image
- Displays it for annotation
- Runs SAM 2 or SAM 3
- Accepts positive and negative clicks
- Saves pixel masks
- Converts masks into YOLO segmentation polygons
- Checks for missing, empty, or invalid labels
- Generates previews for quality control
- Splits the dataset into train, validation, and test sets

Meta’s official SAM 2 implementation accepts points, boxes, and masks as prompts and returns masks at the original image dimensions. It also supports automatic mask generation. [Official Meta SAM 2 repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam2)

However, Codex itself is primarily a reasoning/coding system with image understanding. Official OpenAI documentation describes current models as taking image input and producing text or structured output; it does not document a native ground-truth segmentation-mask output specifically for Codex. [OpenAI model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models)

So:

- **Codex alone looking at the images:** useful for advice, but not dependable for exact pixel boundaries.
- **Codex running SAM:** yes, that can generate real masks.
- **Codex fully labeling everything without review:** technically possible, but scientifically unsafe.

The installed `imagegen` capability should not be used for this - it edits/generates images rather than producing trustworthy ground-truth masks over unchanged originals.

## Why completely automatic annotation will struggle

SAM 2 can segment whatever region you point at, but it does not inherently understand that the region is “fruit damage.”

Its automatic mode may produce masks for:

- The entire fruit
- The background
- Stems
- Shadows
- Highlights
- Natural color patches
- Individual defects

It does not automatically know which masks should be labeled `surface_defect`.

SAM 3 can use text prompts such as “rotten area” or visual examples, which is promising, but subtle bruises and natural fruit coloration remain ambiguous. [Meta SAM 3 overview](https://ai.meta.com/sam3/)

For your particular dataset, “fruit defect” is substantially harder than outlining an ordinary object because the defect:

- Is part of the fruit rather than a separate object
- Can have a fuzzy boundary
- Can resemble normal ripeness or skin coloration
- Looks different across apples, mangoes, bananas, papayas, tomatoes, and Burmese grapes

## Best research-quality workflow

I recommend this process:

1. Manually annotate **50–100 images**, using SAM Smart Annotation to accelerate the outlining.
2. Have another group member review every mask.
3. Train an initial YOLO segmentation model.
4. Use that model to predict masks for the next 200–300 images.
5. Correct those predictions manually.
6. Retrain the model using the expanded dataset.
7. Repeat until the remaining images are pre-annotated.
8. Human-review the final dataset before using it in experiments.

Ultralytics supports using a trained YOLO model to provide annotation predictions and SAM to convert proposed regions into segmentation masks. [Ultralytics auto-annotation documentation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/reference/data/annotator)

This approach is called **human-in-the-loop annotation**. It gives you both speed and defensible research quality.

One caveat: ask your professor whether AI-assisted annotation is permitted. If it is, describe it honestly in the paper:

> Initial defect masks were generated using a promptable segmentation model and subsequently inspected and corrected by human annotators.

My recommendation is **Ultralytics Platform with SAM 2.1 Large or SAM 3**, followed by mandatory manual checking. It is the simplest route for your team and exports cleanly into the segmentation workflow you will probably train with.

how do i manually edit the polygons in cvat


## AI assistant | 2026-09-04 00:23:21

I’ll check CVAT’s current polygon controls so the shortcuts match what you see.

## AI assistant | 2026-09-04 00:23:39

Yes. For an imported polygon:

1. Open the CVAT **job**.
2. Click the polygon to select it.
3. If it is locked, press **L** to unlock it.
4. Zoom in with the mouse wheel.
5. Drag the small polygon points so they follow the visible defect boundary.

Useful controls:

- **Move a point:** drag it.
- **Delete an unnecessary point:** right-click the point → **Delete point**, or hold **Alt** and click it.
- **Fix an entire section:** hold **Shift** and click the polygon, then trace the corrected boundary and connect it to another existing point. Press **Esc** if you mess up.
- **Delete the entire polygon:** select it and press **Delete**.
- **Undo:** **Cmd + Z**.
- **Save:** click the save icon or press **Cmd + S**.

For your fruit dataset, outline only the actual visible defect - such as a bruise, dark rotten patch, cut, mold, or damaged skin. Do not outline the whole fruit unless your professor specifically says the target class is the fruit itself.

## AI assistant | 2026-09-04 07:03:04

Create a **separate polygon for each defect** and assign each polygon its correct class.

For example, if an apple has a bruise and a cut:

- Draw one polygon around the bruise → `bruise_discoloration`
- Draw another polygon around the cut → `cut_crack`

That same image counts as:

- +1 image toward the 300 bruise images
- +1 image toward the 300 cut images

If it has three separate bruises, draw three bruise polygons, but the image still counts only **once** toward the “300 images containing bruises.”

If two defect types overlap and you cannot visually separate them confidently, mark only what is clearly visible and flag the image for team review. Consistency matters more than guessing.
